title: Adaptive Kernel Allocator — operational guide & triage playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This document describes the Adaptive Kernel Allocator (AKA) used by Redwood’s serving runtime, including architecture rationale, kernel scheduling policies, configuration reference, profiling and triage playbook, benchmarking recipes, release-compat notes, known issues, and oncall runbooks. It is intended for engineers who operate the runtime, onboard new kernels, or investigate production latency/cost regressions.

Goals
- Maintain sub-50ms 95th-token latency for short-response workloads on p4d-like instances.
- Reduce wasted GPU cycles by 15% with adaptive packing and kernel-selection.
- Provide clear triage steps that correlate perf regressions to kernel, model, or workload changes.

Audience and ownership
- Primary: serving-runtime team (kernel & scheduling subteam).
- Secondary: eng-sre, infra capacity, benchmarking, and solutions engineers.
- Runbook owner: @Maya Chen (kernel scheduling lead).

Architecture overview
---------------------
The AKA is a lightweight decision layer that sits between the request router and the kernel execution engine. It performs three functions at request time:
1) Match request shape to a kernel (model-architecture, dtype, quantization, seq-length heuristic).
2) Decide packing and batching policy (pack eligible requests vs. start new batch).
3) Select fallback kernels when SLOs or GPU signals indicate degraded performance.

Components (conceptual)
- Selector: rule-engine (static heuristics + learned cost table).
- Profiler cache: recent per-model/per-kernel latency & memory stats (TTL 5m).
- Batcher: continuous batching loop that respects latency budgets (max-wait and max-batch-size).
- Fallback router: dynamic policy that sends heavy requests to cheaper kernels or lower precision variants when error budgets are exceeded.

Kernel selection flow (high level)
1. Request arrives with metadata: model_id, client_tier, max_latency, tokens_remaining, preferred_precision.
2. Selector consults profiler cache; if fresh metrics exist, compute estimated p95.
3. If estimate <= client max_latency and GPU mem available, schedule with primary kernel.
4. Otherwise, evaluate alternatives (quantized kernel, FP16 variant, model-sharded kernel, or lower-batch policy).
5. If no kernel meets latency, consult fallback router for cross-region or lower-cost plan.

Scheduling policies and thresholds
- Default max-wait for interactive workloads: 8ms (<= 100ms target tail).
- Continuous batching target: 80% GPU occupancy for long-form workloads, but no more than client max_latency.
- Prefetch KV-cache window for chat workloads: 3 tokens lookahead to warm KV when sequence extension predicted.
- Memory safety margin: 5% headroom to avoid OOM under jitter.

Configuration reference (examples)
Table: key knobs and recommended values (values used by serving-prod prod-ops)
- selector.cost_model_ttl: 300s
- batcher.max_wait_ms: 8
- batcher.max_batch_size: 64 (per-GPU dependent; p4: 64, a100-40: 96)
- allocator.mem_headroom_pct: 5
- fallback.p95_budget_pct: 120
- quantization.allowed: [int8, int4] (per-model opt-in)

Example YAML for a model routing profile:
----
model_routing:
  model_id: gptx-3.2b
  primary_kernel: fused-attn-fp16
  allowed_kernels: [fused-attn-fp16, fused-attn-int8, sharded-attn-fp16]
  batch_policy:
    max_wait_ms: 6
    max_batch_size: 48
  sla_token_p95_ms: 60
  profiling_tier: high-frequency
----

Operational playbook: triage step-by-step
---------------------------------------
When a performance regression is reported (SLO alert or customer ticket):
1) Capture the alert context: model_id, route, region, time window, and token-level latency histogram.
2) Check selector.profiler cache for recent kernel metrics and compare last 24h baseline. (CLI: rwdctl runtime profiler --model gptx-3.2b --since 24h).
3) Run a targeted perf capture (2x warmup runs, 5 measured requests) using the runtime trace collector.
   - Command: rwdctl trace collect --route <route> --model <model_id> --warmup 2 --runs 5 --output /tmp/trace.json
4) If the trace shows kernel-level slowdown (spikes in kernel exec time): open an issue annotated with kernel name, invocation args, GPU metrics (SM util, memory allocs).
5) If batch build-up is high (requests coalesced beyond expected batch size), check batcher.max_wait_ms and rate-limiter/backpressure settings.
6) If memory pressure preceded slowdown, capture dGPU memory timeline: (nvidia-smi sample with timestamps) and compare with allocator logs.
7) Apply mitigation: reduce batcher.max_wait_ms by 50% for the affected route and deploy a canary (see rollout steps).
8) Post-mortem: add new workload example to benchmarking-suite and schedule a kernel re-evaluation.

Profiling playbook (detailed)
- Low-noise microbenchmarks: run the kernel microbench harness on the same instance type as reported in-prod: 
  ./bench/kernel_microbench --kernel fused-attn-fp16 --seq_len 128 --batch 32 --dtype fp16
  Capture lacquer: output CSV with 99th percentile, median, and allocs.
- Request-level trace collection: enable token-level timestamps and KV-cache events. Use rwdctl trace analyze to get waterfall charts.
- Correlate with host metrics: GPU SM util, PCIe throughput, CPU steal, and syscalls per-second. An example sequence to collect correlated metrics:
  1) start rwd-metrics agent: sudo systemctl start rwd-metrics
  2) collect for window: rwdctl metrics collect --duration 120s --out /tmp/metrics.json
  3) analyze: rwdctl trace correlate --trace /tmp/trace.json --metrics /tmp/metrics.json
- Common perf fingerprints and probable causes:
  - Longer kernel exec times, normal SM util: kernel regression (new kernel build or ISA change).
  - Lower SM util with high queue depth: batcher packing inefficiency or GIL-like scheduling stalls.
  - Memory spike followed by OOM/slowdown: unexpected model growth (new tokenizer) or KV-cache leak.

Benchmarking recipes (benchmarks used to validate kernel changes)
- Synthetic microbench suite: measure: p50/p95 exec time, memory alloc, launch overhead. Key commands: 
  - bench-run --suite micro --kernel fused-attn-fp16 --iters 200
- Real-world request replay: replay production traces with preserved timing (use bench-replay tool):
  - bench-replay --trace traces/2025-01-18-prod.json --scale 1.0 --out results/replay-20250118.json
- Regression gating: new kernel builds must pass:
  1) microbench p95 <= baseline_p95 * 1.05
  2) replay tail latency no worse than baseline + 10ms at 95th
  3) memory alloc <= baseline * 1.02

Release notes (short)
- AKA v2.7.0 (2025-01-30): improved selector cost model to include PCIe transfer estimates; default batcher.max_wait_ms reduced to 8ms for interactive routes.
- AKA v2.6.0 (2024-10-12): added quantized kernel routing and per-model profiling_tier flag.

Known issues (operational)
- ISSUE #1234: Quantized kernel int8 may underperform for short seqs on a100-40 when batch_size < 8. Mitigation: force fp16 for seq<32 or batch<8.
- ISSUE #1291: Profiler cache TTL expiration sometimes leaves stale metrics during sudden traffic spikes. Workaround: flush selector.profiler cache on deploy: rwdctl runtime flush-profiler --model <id>.
- ISSUE #1305: Rare deadlock when two concurrent batchers attempt to grow the same dynamic scratch buffer. Symptoms: throughput drop, increased p95. Hotfix: AKA v2.7.0 includes an optimistic mem-reservation strategy.

Runbook: immediate mitigation checklist
1) If SLO alert triggers: add temporary route override to use primary_kernel: fused-attn-fp16, batcher.max_wait_ms: 4, and scale replicas +20%.
   - CLI: rwdctl route apply --route <route> --override-file /tmp/override.yml
2) If OOMs observed: set allocator.mem_headroom_pct to 10% and restart the allocator agent on affected hosts.
3) If sustained tail latency only on one zone: failover traffic to next-best zone and engage infra for instance health.
4) Always capture traces and push to /artifacts/runtime-traces/<incident-id>/ before changing configs.

Canary/rollout guidance
- New kernel builds must be rolled out via staged canary: 2 hosts (1% traffic) -> 10 hosts (10% traffic) -> 50 hosts (50%) -> full. Monitor: p50/p95, GPU SM util, memory alloc, and request errors. Gate at each stage with 15 minute observation window and automated rollback on 5% relative p95 increase.

Operational alerts to define
- kernel.exec_time.p95 > baseline * 1.2 for 5m
- batcher.queue_depth > max_batch_size * 3 for 2m
- allocator.mem_headroom < 1% for any host for 1m
- kernel.errors.rate > 0.5% for 10m

Ownership and escalations
- First-line: serving-runtime oncall (primary).
- Second-line: kernel team (for kernel-level regressions) and eng-sre (for infra resource constraints).
- Pager: paging policy: P1 if customer-visible SLO breach; escalate to oncall manager after 30 minutes.

Team wiki / how to onboard new engineers
- Read the runtime-architecture primer, then run the microbench harness locally.
- Exercise: add a synthetic kernel (simulated exec times) and validate that selector chooses it under appropriate config.
- Checklists: local dev environment: docker image rwd/runtime-dev:latest, bench tools in /tools/bench.

References and links
- Kernel test harness (internal): git://redwood/serving/kernel-harness
- Benchmarks and replay traces: /data/benchmarks/prod-traces
- Incident template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

Appendix: quick commands
- Flush profiler cache for a model: rwdctl runtime flush-profiler --model gptx-3.2b
- Collect a 10-request trace: rwdctl trace collect --route chat-prod --model gptx-3.2b --warmup 2 --runs 10 --out /tmp/t.json
- Run microbench: ./tools/bench/kernel_microbench --kernel fused-attn-fp16 --seq_len 128 --batch 32 --iters 200
